title: Seeing in the Dark
summary: Find out something is wrong before your users tell you — and where: metrics, structured logs, distributed traces, SLOs and alerts that matter.

goals.text: Watch every service with RED and USE metrics
Follow one request across services with a trace
Alert on symptoms with SLOs and burn rates
Keep telemetry cost and cardinality in check

steps.title: Users noticed first
body: Quillmail sends newsletters for independent writers: a gateway, Lists, Send, Billing and a Templates service that renders each issue.
At 14:02 a new template engine went out. For two hours, 3% of newsletters silently failed to send. The team found out when a writer complained publicly — that's the only alerting system they had.

card.title: What the team saw
lines: 16:05  a writer posts: “my issue never went out”
! 3% of sends failing for two hours

steps.title: Searching 14 machines by hand
body: The on-call engineer logs into machines one by one and greps text files. Messages are vague, formats differ per service, and nothing links a log line to the request that caused it.

Hours go by just working out which service is failing. Observability is the ability to answer new questions about a running system from the data it emits — and right now it emits almost nothing useful.

card.title: send-07: /var/log/app.log
lines: # 14 machines, different formats, no request ids
! which of these is our problem?

steps.title: A few numbers for everything
body: Metrics are cheap numeric time series. For every service that handles requests, track RED: request Rate, Error rate and Duration (as percentiles). For every resource — CPU, disk, queue, pool — track USE: Utilization, Saturation and Errors.
A dashboard of those answers “is something wrong, and roughly where?” in seconds: Send's errors and p99 jumped at 14:02; Lists didn't move.

steps.title: Logs a machine can query
body: Structured logs write each event as fields (JSON) rather than prose: service, level, request id, list, error, duration. Shipped to one central store, they can be filtered and counted like a database.
One query shows that 98% of Send's errors are “render timeout” — the problem is downstream of Send.
changes: ~ Logs are JSON with request ids
~ All logs in one searchable store

card.title: One event = one JSON line
lines: # query: svc=send AND err=* | count by err

steps.title: Follow one request end to end
body: A distributed trace follows a single request through every service. The gateway assigns a trace id and passes it along in headers; each service records spans — what it did, when, for how long, and for which parent.
Laid out as a waterfall, trace r-7f3a points straight at it: 1.92 of its 2.1 seconds are spent in templates.render.

card.title: Trace r-7f3a · 2.1 s
lines: # each span: service, start, duration, parent

steps.title: The pager that cried wolf
body: Dashboards need someone watching, so the team adds alerts: CPU above 80%, disk above 70%, any error log. The pager goes off 40 times a week; almost every page is harmless.
Engineers start ignoring it — and a real incident sits unacknowledged for 45 minutes. Alerts on causes are noisy, because systems routinely run hot without hurting anyone.

card.title: Alerting on causes
lines: # people learn to ignore the pager

steps.title: Promise something users care about
body: Alert on symptoms instead. Pick a service level indicator (SLI) users feel: the share of issues sent within 60 s. Set a service level objective (SLO): 99.9% over 30 days.
That leaves an error budget of 0.1% — about 43 minutes of full outage a month. Small blips spend a little budget and wake nobody; anything that threatens the promise pages.

card.title: Alert on what users feel
lines: SLI: issues accepted and sent within 60 s
# page only when the budget burns fast

steps.title: How fast is the budget going?
body: The burn rate compares how fast you're spending the error budget with the pace that would use exactly all of it in 30 days. At 1× all is well; at 14× the month's budget is gone in about two days — page now. A slow 6× burn becomes a ticket for working hours.
Check a long and a short window together, so a brief spike doesn't page and a recovered incident stops paging quickly.

card.title: Burn rate → action
lines: # check a long and a short window together

steps.title: The same incident, with eyes
body: Rewind to the bad deploy, with everything in place. Two minutes in, the send SLO burns at 30× and pages. The dashboard shows only Send unhealthy; a trace shows Templates rendering for 1.9 s. Rollback at 14:09.
Detection went from 2 hours to 2 minutes, diagnosis from 4 hours to 5 minutes — and a writer never had to tell anyone.

card.title: The same bug, replayed
lines: 14:05  dashboard: only send errors, p99 up

steps.title: Seeing everything costs money
body: Telemetry has a bill. Each unique combination of metric labels is a separate time series, so a label like user_id creates millions — a cardinality explosion. Keep per-user detail in logs and traces.
Traces are usually sampled: keep, say, 1% of normal requests plus every error and slow one. Logs need levels and retention limits. Spend where it answers questions.

card.title: Telemetry has a bill
lines: ! high-cardinality ids go in logs and traces, not metric labels

steps.title: Know before they tell you
body:
• Metrics (RED for services, USE for resources) say whether and roughly where.
  • Structured, centralised logs say what happened to a request.
  • Traces show where the time went across services.
  • Alert on symptoms via SLOs and burn rate, not on every cause.
  • Watch cardinality and sample traces to keep the bill sane.
